$comment: What a source says about a muscle in an animal, before anyone has decided which homology group it belongs to. An occurrence has to sit inside a muscle record, so until now an observation whose record was unsettled had nowhere to live and mining was gated on homology — which meant a paper had to be read again once the homology was worked out. This file removes that gate: extract everything a source states, put here whatever cannot yet be assigned, and promote rows into records as the synonymies are settled. Nothing here is counted in coverage; these are observations waiting for a home, not rows. See docs/SCHEMA.md.

blockedBy.nomenclature: The source's name for the muscle cannot yet be matched to a record — usually an older or a taxon-specific nomenclature with no stated synonymy.
blockedBy.homology: The muscle is identified but which record it belongs to is an open question in the literature.
blockedBy.no-record: The muscle has no record in this dataset yet, and creating one needs a cross-taxon treatment that has not been read.
blockedBy.division: The source splits or fuses a muscle differently from the record, and which part maps where is unsettled.
blockedBy.partial: The source states a difference, an extent or a variation rather than a complete attachment — 'the origin ranges from the lateral half in Testudo to the lateral fifth in Emys'. The record is usually known; what needs judgement is whether the statement stands as an occurrence on its own or only refines one.
blockedBy.occupied: The record already carries a row for this species from another worker, and the dataset holds one row per (record, species). Two independent descriptions of one animal do not conflict — METHODS is explicit that an attachment is an observation and does not age — but merging them into one row, or deciding which worker's reading the row should state, is judgement.

observations.attachmentNote: This muscle’s tendinous origin is located further distally on the ventral epicondyle of the humerus than that of M. pronator superficialis, and is associated with a relatively deep circular pit on the bone. It has a fleshy insertion on the proximal ventral radial shaft, extending for approximately one fifth the length of the radius. The insertion extends slightly further distally than that of M. pronator superficialis, and is demarcated by intermuscular lines. (The avian dorsal epicondyle is the ectepicondyle and the ventral epicondyle the entepicondyle. Prose only — the structured rows wait on the record, not on another reading.)

observations.name: M. propatagialis
observations.blockedNote: **The propatagial complex has no record in this dataset.** Widrig et al. describe it in full and figure it (their Fig. 10), and Fisher & Goodman's tensor patagii longus and brevis are parked on the same gap — so two sources now describe the same structure with nowhere to put it. That is enough to justify creating the record; what it needs first is a decision about whether the propatagialis is one homology group or several, and whether `humeroradialis` — which carries 'M. tensor propatagialis' as a *Chauna* name — is part of it or a different muscle.
observations.attachmentNote: This muscle is unique to the avian lineage, and its developmental origin is tied to muscle progenitor cells originating from the developing Mm. deltoideus major, pectoralis, biceps brachii, and extensor carpi radialis (Uno and Hirasawa 2023; Uno and Hirasawa 2025). The origin point of this muscle is located on the dorsal apex of the furcular head, which corresponds to a rugose area on the bone. It extends superficial to the muscles of the proximal humerus, overlying Mm. deltoideus major, deltoideus minor, and coracobrachialis cranialis as a broad, thin sheet. Fibers from the sheath covering the main body of M. pectoralis wrap over the deltopectoral crest to join the body of M. propatagialis, representing the so-called “M. pectoralis propatagialis” of some authors. The elongated, tendinous portion of M. propatagialis that inserts on the carpometacarpus branches off from the broader, sheetlike portion of the muscle just distal to the deltopectoral crest. The so-called “biceps slip” connects the sheetlike portion of the muscle to M. biceps brachii near the approximate midpoint of the humeral shaft. The tendinous portion of M. propatagialis receives additional fibers from the proximal fleshy belly of M. ex- tensor carpi radialis. It extends down the leading edge of the wing encased by a tube of thickened dermis, and inserts immediately ventral to M. extensor carpi radialis on the proximal portion of the extensor process, which in anhimids is elongated into a large spur. An elongate scar corresponds to the insertions of this muscle and those of Mm. extensor carpi radialis and extensor longus alulae. (The avian dorsal epicondyle is the ectepicondyle and the ventral epicondyle the entepicondyle. Prose only — the structured rows wait on the record, not on another reading.)

observations.name: M. ulnometacarpalis dorsalis
observations.blockedNote: See M. ulnometacarpalis ventralis.
observations.attachmentNote: The tendon of origin for this muscle stretches across the caudal surface of the distal head of the ulna, where it leaves a clear impression on the bone surrounded by intermuscular lines. The muscle belly crosses the wrist and inserts fleshily on the proximalmost portion of the minor metacarpal, where it leaves no osteological correlate. (The avian dorsal epicondyle is the ectepicondyle and the ventral epicondyle the entepicondyle. Prose only — the structured rows wait on the record, not on another reading.)

observations.name: M. ulnometacarpalis ventralis
observations.blockedNote: One of the avian ulnometacarpales, which this dataset has no record for. They are intrinsic to the avian forearm-to-hand transfer and have no obvious cross-tetrapod counterpart.
observations.attachmentNote: The distal cranial ulnar shaft is the site of this muscle's fleshy origin, which is bounded by intermuscular lines. It crosses the wrist as a thick tendon through a clearly defined notch on the ventral side of the radiale identified by Mayr (2014) and inserts on the proximal cranial carpometacarpus, where it does not leave any osteological correlates. (The avian dorsal epicondyle is the ectepicondyle and the ventral epicondyle the entepicondyle. Prose only — the structured rows wait on the record, not on another reading.)
